concepts.name: Linear combinations
concepts.summary: Scale some vectors and add them up. Multiplying a matrix by a vector does exactly this to the matrix's columns.

equations.says: A times x adds up the columns of A, each scaled by an entry of x.

metaphors.name: A recipe
metaphors.says: The ingredients are the vectors and the amounts are the x. Two cups of one and half a cup of another is a linear combination of the two.

metaphors.name: Directions on a grid
metaphors.says: "Three blocks east, two blocks north" reaches an address by scaling two steps and adding them.

metaphors.name: A mixing desk
metaphors.says: Each fader scales one track, and the speakers play their sum.

applications.name: Screen color
applications.says: Every pixel is some amount of red, green and blue light added together.

applications.name: Facial animation
applications.says: A character's expression is a weighted mix of sculpted blend shapes: so much smile, so much frown.

applications.name: Neural networks
applications.says: Each neuron starts by taking a weighted sum of its inputs.

applications.name: Audio mixing
applications.says: A mixdown is each channel times its gain, added up.

concepts.name: Row and column pictures
concepts.summary: Two ways to see a system of equations. Each row is a line (or a plane) and the solution is where they all cross; or the right side is a combination of the columns, and the solution says how much of each.

equations.says: Row picture: two lines that cross at (2, 3).
Column picture: 2 of the first column plus 3 of the second make the right side.

metaphors.name: Clues in a mystery
metaphors.says: Each clue rules out all but a line of suspects; the answer is the one every clue allows. That is the row picture.

metaphors.name: Making change
metaphors.says: How many quarters and how many dimes make 85 cents? The coins are the columns and the counts are the solution. That is the column picture.

metaphors.name: One city, two maps
metaphors.says: A street map and a transit map show the same place; each answers different questions more easily.

applications.name: Positioning
applications.says: GPS finds a receiver where the surfaces of equal distance from each satellite cross: the row picture.

applications.name: Collision detection
applications.says: Where two lines or planes in a scene meet is the solution of their equations.

applications.name: Blending
applications.says: How much of each feed, alloy or fuel to mix to hit a target composition is the column picture.

applications.name: Robot arms
applications.says: Which joint speeds combine to move the hand in a given direction.

concepts.name: Elimination
concepts.summary: Subtract multiples of one equation from the ones below it until the system is triangular, then solve from the bottom up. The first nonzero entry left in each row is a pivot.

equations.says: The multiplier: how many of the pivot row j to subtract from row i to put a zero under the pivot.
Elimination turns A into an upper triangular U, and b into c, without changing the solution.

metaphors.name: Solving a logic puzzle
metaphors.says: Use one clue to simplify the others until one of them gives an answer outright.

metaphors.name: Climbing back up a staircase
metaphors.says: Once the system is triangular, the bottom step names one unknown, which unlocks the step above it, and so on up.

metaphors.name: Fair trades
metaphors.says: Subtracting a multiple of one equation from another keeps the books balanced, the way adding the same weight to both pans keeps a scale level.

applications.name: Circuit simulators
applications.says: Tools like SPICE turn a circuit into equations for its node voltages and eliminate.

applications.name: Structural engineering
applications.says: Finite element models of bridges and buildings are huge linear systems, solved by elimination tuned for sparse matrices.

applications.name: Numerical libraries
applications.says: The linear solvers under NumPy, MATLAB and R are elimination at heart.

applications.name: Erasure codes
applications.says: Storage systems and QR codes rebuild missing data by eliminating over a finite field.

concepts.name: Matrix multiplication
concepts.summary: Each entry of a product is a row of the first matrix times a column of the second. Doing B and then A to a vector is the same as doing AB once.

equations.says: Entry i, j of AB is row i of A dotted with column j of B.
Multiplying is associative, so a product of matrices is one step that does all of theirs.

metaphors.name: A bakery's orders
metaphors.says: A table of ingredients per recipe times a table of recipes per day gives ingredients per day: each entry is a row times a column.

metaphors.name: An assembly line
metaphors.says: Each station does one step; bolting the stations together makes one machine that does all of them.

metaphors.name: Converting currency twice
metaphors.says: Dollars to euros, then euros to yen, is the same as one rate from dollars to yen.

applications.name: Graphics pipelines
applications.says: Model, camera and projection transforms are multiplied into one matrix, so each vertex is transformed once.

applications.name: Deep learning
applications.says: Every layer is a matrix product; GPUs and TPUs are built to do them fast.

applications.name: Counting paths
applications.says: The powers of a graph's adjacency matrix count the walks between every pair of nodes.

applications.name: Databases and spreadsheets
applications.says: Joining a table of users to items with a table of items to features is a matrix product.

concepts.name: Inverse matrices
concepts.summary: The inverse undoes what a matrix does. A square matrix has one exactly when elimination finds a full set of pivots; Gauss–Jordan elimination finds it.

equations.says: The inverse undoes A, from either side.
To undo two steps, undo the last one first.
Gauss–Jordan: the row operations that turn A into I turn I into the inverse.

metaphors.name: An undo button
metaphors.says: Do A, then its inverse, and you are back where you started.

metaphors.name: Socks and shoes
metaphors.says: To undo putting on socks and then shoes, take off the shoes first: the inverse of AB is B⁻¹ then A⁻¹.

metaphors.name: Scrambled eggs
metaphors.says: A singular matrix is like scrambling an egg: information is lost, and nothing can undo it.

applications.name: Picking in 3D
applications.says: Turning a mouse click back into a ray in the world uses the inverse of the camera's transforms.

applications.name: Robot frames
applications.says: Knowing where the camera sits on a robot, the inverse transform takes what the camera sees into the robot's own coordinates.

applications.name: Classical ciphers
applications.says: The Hill cipher encrypts letters by a matrix and decrypts by its inverse.

applications.name: Knowing when not to
applications.says: Numerical code rarely forms an inverse: solving with elimination is faster and more accurate.

concepts.name: LU factorization
concepts.summary: Elimination, recorded. The multipliers fill a lower triangular L, and what elimination leaves is an upper triangular U, so solving with a new right side is two quick triangular solves.

equations.says: L holds the multipliers under ones on its diagonal; U holds the pivots on its diagonal.
Solve forward for c, then back for x.

metaphors.name: Meal prep
metaphors.says: Do the chopping once on Sunday, and every dinner that week is quick.

metaphors.name: A stencil
metaphors.says: Cutting the stencil is the slow part; painting with it again is fast.

metaphors.name: A receipt
metaphors.says: L is the record of every step elimination took, so the work never has to be repeated.

applications.name: Many loads, one structure
applications.says: Engineers test a bridge under many loads; the matrix stays the same, so it is factored once.

applications.name: Simulation time steps
applications.says: Implicit physics and circuit solvers often face the same matrix every step and reuse its factors.

applications.name: Determinants
applications.says: The determinant is the product of U's diagonal, which is how libraries compute it.

applications.name: Everyday solvers
applications.says: NumPy's solve and MATLAB's backslash factor into LU, with row swaps, behind the scenes.

concepts.name: Transposes and permutations
concepts.summary: The transpose flips a matrix across its diagonal, so rows become columns. A permutation matrix reorders rows; it is what elimination needs when a zero sits where a pivot should be.

equations.says: The transpose swaps rows for columns.
Transposing a product reverses its order.
With rows exchanged first, every invertible matrix has an LU factorization.
Undoing a reordering is reordering back.

metaphors.name: Turning a spreadsheet sideways
metaphors.says: Rows become columns: a table of students by subjects becomes subjects by students.

metaphors.name: Who sent and who received
metaphors.says: If a table says who emailed whom, its transpose says who was emailed by whom.

metaphors.name: Shuffling a deck
metaphors.says: A permutation reorders without changing any card, and every shuffle can be undone.

applications.name: Backpropagation
applications.says: Gradients flow backwards through a network's layers by the transposes of their weight matrices.

applications.name: Memory layout
applications.says: Row-major and column-major storage are transposes of each other; libraries transpose to keep reads cache-friendly.

applications.name: Pivoting
applications.says: Solvers swap rows to put the largest available entry in the pivot position, which keeps rounding errors small.

applications.name: Sorting and shuffling
applications.says: A sort finds the permutation that puts data in order; a shuffle applies a random one.

concepts.name: Vector spaces and subspaces
concepts.summary: A set of vectors you can't leave by adding or scaling. A subspace is one inside another: a line or a plane through the origin, never one that misses it.

equations.says: Every combination of vectors in the space is in the space too.

metaphors.name: A closed club
metaphors.says: Any mix of members is a member: there is no combination that takes you outside.

metaphors.name: A sheet of glass through the origin
metaphors.says: Slide and stretch along it however you like and you stay on it. A sheet that misses the origin is not closed: double a point and you fall off.

metaphors.name: Sounds
metaphors.says: Add two sounds, or turn one up, and you have another sound. Functions are vectors too.

applications.name: Audio and signals
applications.says: Mixing and filtering work because signals can be added and scaled like vectors.

applications.name: Error-correcting codes
applications.says: A linear code is a subspace: the sum of two codewords is a codeword, which makes decoding systematic.

applications.name: Embeddings
applications.says: Search and language models place words and images in a vector space where directions carry meaning.

applications.name: Superposition
applications.says: Solutions of linear circuits and vibrating systems form a vector space, so responses to separate inputs simply add.

concepts.name: Column space
concepts.summary: All the combinations of a matrix's columns: every vector A can reach. Ax = b has a solution exactly when b is in it.

equations.says: The column space is everything A times a vector can be.
A right side outside it has no solution.

metaphors.name: The paints you own
metaphors.says: Every color you can mix from them is in the column space. A color outside it cannot be made, however you mix.

metaphors.name: A crane on rails
metaphors.says: The rails decide which spots the hook can reach.

metaphors.name: A projector's screen
metaphors.says: Whatever slide you feed in, the picture lands somewhere on the screen.

applications.name: Best fits
applications.says: When b is out of reach, least squares finds the closest point in the column space.

applications.name: Controllability
applications.says: Control engineers ask which states a system's inputs can steer it to: a column space.

applications.name: Recommendations
applications.says: If ratings come from a few tastes, the ratings matrix lives in a small column space, which recommenders exploit.

applications.name: Drawing 3D on a screen
applications.says: A projection sends every point of a scene into a plane: its column space.

concepts.name: Nullspace
concepts.summary: Every x that A sends to zero. Elimination finds it: each free column gives one special solution, and their combinations are the whole nullspace.

equations.says: The nullspace is what A flattens to zero.
One special solution for each of the n − r free variables.

metaphors.name: Moves the machine can't see
metaphors.says: Spinning a perfectly round ball changes nothing anyone can see; those moves are in the nullspace.

metaphors.name: A camera's blind direction
metaphors.says: Every point along a ray from the lens lands on the same pixel. Moving along the ray is invisible to the camera.

metaphors.name: Balanced trades
metaphors.says: Adding the same weight to both pans of a scale leaves the needle where it was.

applications.name: Balancing chemical equations
applications.says: The coefficients that balance a reaction are a vector in a nullspace.

applications.name: Redundant robots
applications.says: An arm with extra joints can move them in the nullspace to dodge obstacles while its hand stays still.

applications.name: Camera geometry
applications.says: Computer vision estimates a camera's matrix from point matches by finding a nullspace vector.

applications.name: Circuit loops
applications.says: Currents that circulate around loops without piling up at any node form a nullspace.

concepts.name: Rank and the complete solution
concepts.summary: The rank is the number of pivots: how many independent rows, and as many independent columns. Every solution of Ax = b is one particular solution plus something from the nullspace.

equations.says: Rank counts the equations that really say something new.
A particular solution, plus any vector A sends to zero.

metaphors.name: Independent witnesses
metaphors.says: A witness who repeats another's story adds no information. The rank counts the witnesses worth hearing.

metaphors.name: Knobs wired together
metaphors.says: A mixing desk with ten knobs, half of them wired to the others, really has five controls.

metaphors.name: A route plus a round trip
metaphors.says: Any way to the party is one known route plus some loop that brings you back to where you were.

applications.name: Redundant features
applications.says: In statistics a design matrix that isn't full rank means some features repeat others, and the fit is ambiguous.

applications.name: Compression
applications.says: A low-rank table is described by far fewer numbers than it has entries.

applications.name: Rigid frames
applications.says: The rank of a frame's rigidity matrix says whether it holds its shape or wobbles.

applications.name: Structure from motion
applications.says: Tracked points in a video form a matrix of low rank, which recovers the 3D shape and the camera's path.

concepts.name: Independence, basis and dimension
concepts.summary: Vectors are independent when none is a combination of the others. A basis is an independent set that spans the space, and every basis of a space has the same number of vectors: its dimension.

equations.says: Independent: the only combination that gives zero is the one with nothing in it.

metaphors.name: Primary colors
metaphors.says: A small set that mixes into everything, with none of them a mix of the others.

metaphors.name: A coordinate system
metaphors.says: East, north and up: three directions, none a combination of the other two, that name every place.

metaphors.name: Degrees of freedom
metaphors.says: A bead on a wire has one, an ant on a table two, a fly in a room three. That count is the dimension.

applications.name: Feature selection
applications.says: Dropping features that are combinations of others removes redundancy before training a model.

applications.name: Camera frames
applications.says: A graphics camera keeps a basis of right, up and forward to place everything it sees.

applications.name: Robot design
applications.says: A six-joint arm has six degrees of freedom, just enough to place and orient a hand in space.

applications.name: Model size
applications.says: The dimension of a space of curves or signals is how many numbers it takes to describe one.

concepts.name: The four fundamental subspaces
concepts.summary: An m by n matrix has four subspaces: its column space and left nullspace in m dimensions, its row space and nullspace in n. Their dimensions are fixed by the rank, and each pair meets at right angles.

equations.says: The column space and the row space have the same dimension: the rank.

equations.tex: \dim N(A) = n - r, \qquad \dim N(A^{\mathsf T}) = m - r
equations.says: The nullspaces fill out the rest of each side.

equations.tex: N(A) \perp C(A^{\mathsf T}), \qquad N(A^{\mathsf T}) \perp C(A)
equations.says: Each nullspace is perpendicular to the space beside it.

metaphors.name: A camera, fully described
metaphors.says: What parts of a scene it responds to (row space), what motions it can't see (nullspace), what pictures it can take (column space), and what pictures are impossible.

metaphors.name: Accounting checks
metaphors.says: The left nullspace holds the rules every honest b must pass, like the rule that debits equal credits.

metaphors.name: Two rooms, two walls
metaphors.says: Each side of the matrix is a room split by a right-angled wall: the part that matters and the part that is lost.

applications.name: Kirchhoff's laws
applications.says: For a circuit's incidence matrix, the subspaces are exactly the voltage law, the current law and the loops.

applications.name: Parity checks
applications.says: An error-correcting code checks a message against vectors orthogonal to every codeword; any nonzero check means an error.

applications.name: Least squares and the SVD
applications.says: Both are built on splitting each side into these perpendicular pieces.

applications.name: Understanding a model
applications.says: The nullspace of a linear model shows which inputs it ignores entirely.

concepts.name: Rank one matrices
concepts.summary: A column times a row. Every one of its columns is a multiple of the same vector, and any matrix of rank r is a sum of r of them.

equations.says: Rank one: the column u, scaled by each entry of the row v.

metaphors.name: A multiplication table
metaphors.says: Every entry is its row label times its column label: the simplest rank one matrix.

metaphors.name: Plaid
metaphors.says: One stripe across times one stripe down makes a plaid. Any pattern is a sum of plaids, and the rank is how many it takes.

metaphors.name: Transparencies
metaphors.says: A picture built from a stack of simple layers, each a column times a row.

applications.name: Image compression
applications.says: Keeping the few strongest rank one layers of an image keeps most of what the eye sees.

applications.name: Recommenders
applications.says: The simplest model of ratings is a user's taste times an item's appeal: rank one.

applications.name: Fine-tuning language models
applications.says: LoRA adapts a large model by adding low-rank updates instead of changing every weight.

applications.name: Gradients
applications.says: For one training example, a layer's weight gradient is a column times a row.

concepts.name: Graphs and incidence matrices
concepts.summary: A graph of nodes and edges as a matrix: a row per edge, with −1 where it leaves and +1 where it arrives. Its subspaces are the graph's own facts: potentials, currents that balance, and loops.

equations.says: Kirchhoff's current law: the flow into each node is the flow out.
Euler's formula for a connected graph, from the dimensions of the subspaces.

metaphors.name: One-way roads
metaphors.says: Each road leaves one town and enters another: a −1 and a +1 in its row.

metaphors.name: Water pipes
metaphors.says: At every junction what flows in must flow out. Flows that balance are in the left nullspace.

metaphors.name: Heights on a hike
metaphors.says: Only differences in height matter to how steep a path is, so lifting every height by the same amount changes nothing.

applications.name: Circuit analysis
applications.says: Kirchhoff's laws are the incidence matrix and its transpose.

applications.name: Network flow
applications.says: Shipping, traffic and data routing are flows on a graph, constrained by its incidence matrix.

applications.name: Spectral clustering
applications.says: The graph Laplacian AᵀA reveals clusters of tightly connected nodes.

applications.name: Mesh processing
applications.says: Graphics computes gradients and smoothing on 3D meshes through their incidence matrices.

concepts.name: Orthogonal vectors and subspaces
concepts.summary: Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero: they meet at a right angle. Two subspaces are orthogonal when every vector of one is orthogonal to every vector of the other.

equations.says: Orthogonal: the dot product is zero.
Pythagoras holds exactly when x and y are orthogonal.

metaphors.name: North and east
metaphors.says: Walking east never changes how far north you are.

metaphors.name: Bass and treble
metaphors.says: Two knobs that don't interfere: turning one leaves the other's effect alone.

metaphors.name: A noon shadow
metaphors.says: A pole standing straight up casts no shadow on the ground, because it shares nothing with the ground's directions.

applications.name: Lighting
applications.says: Brightness on a surface is the dot product of its normal and the light's direction; at right angles it is dark.

applications.name: Similarity search
applications.says: Search engines compare documents and embeddings by the angle between them; orthogonal means unrelated.

applications.name: Shared radio channels
applications.says: CDMA gives each phone an orthogonal code so many can talk at once without interfering.

applications.name: Wi-Fi subcarriers
applications.says: OFDM packs many orthogonal carriers into one channel.

concepts.name: Projections
concepts.summary: The closest point to b on a line or a subspace, found by dropping a perpendicular. The error left over is orthogonal to the subspace.

equations.says: Projecting b onto the line through a.
The matrix that projects onto the column space of A.
Projecting twice changes nothing more.

metaphors.name: A shadow at noon
metaphors.says: Light from straight overhead throws each point straight down onto the floor.

metaphors.name: The nearest point on a road
metaphors.says: Walk straight to the road, at a right angle, and you take the shortest path to it.

metaphors.name: A headline
metaphors.says: Keeps the part of the story that fits, and drops what doesn't.

applications.name: Sliding along walls
applications.says: Game physics projects out the part of a velocity that points into a wall, so a character slides along it.

applications.name: Shadows and orthographic views
applications.says: Graphics flattens objects onto planes for shadows and technical drawings.

applications.name: Denoising
applications.says: Projecting a signal onto a space of smooth signals removes much of its noise.

applications.name: Dimensionality reduction
applications.says: PCA projects data onto its few most important directions.

concepts.name: Least squares
concepts.summary: When Ax = b has no solution, solve for the x that comes closest: the one whose error is orthogonal to the column space. Fitting a line to scattered points is the classic case.

equations.says: The normal equations: the best x makes the error orthogonal to every column.
Best means the sum of squared errors is as small as it can be.

metaphors.name: Splitting the difference
metaphors.says: Ask five friends the time and average their answers: the average is a least-squares fit.

metaphors.name: A ruler through dots
metaphors.says: Lay a ruler through scattered dots so that it misses all of them as little as possible.

metaphors.name: A fair compromise
metaphors.says: No one gets exactly what they asked for, but the total disappointment is as small as it can be.

applications.name: Regression
applications.says: Linear regression in statistics and machine learning is least squares.

applications.name: GPS
applications.says: A receiver hears more satellites than it needs and takes the position that fits them all best.

applications.name: Calibration
applications.says: Sensors and cameras are calibrated by fitting their parameters to many measurements.

applications.name: Curve fitting
applications.says: Drawing apps smooth a shaky stroke by fitting a curve to the points of the mouse.

concepts.name: Orthonormal bases and Gram–Schmidt
concepts.summary: Vectors of length one at right angles to each other are the easiest basis to work in. Gram–Schmidt makes one from any basis, by subtracting from each vector its projections onto the ones before.

equations.says: The columns of Q are orthonormal.
Take away what b has along the earlier directions, then scale what is left to length one.
Gram–Schmidt as a factorization: R is upper triangular.

metaphors.name: Hiring without overlap
metaphors.says: Each new hire is given only the work no one already covers.

metaphors.name: Squaring a frame
metaphors.says: Fix one side, then make each next side square to all the ones before.

metaphors.name: Hearing a new voice
metaphors.says: Take away what a new speaker repeats from earlier ones, and what is left is what they add.

applications.name: QR factorization
applications.says: The orthonormal Q from Gram–Schmidt solves least-squares problems stably.

applications.name: Camera look-at
applications.says: A graphics camera builds its right and up directions perpendicular to the way it faces.

applications.name: Large eigenproblems
applications.says: Krylov methods such as Arnoldi and Lanczos orthogonalize as they go to find eigenvalues of huge sparse matrices.

applications.name: Signal bases
applications.says: Orthogonal sets of signals let a receiver pull each one out of a mix with a dot product.

concepts.name: Properties of the determinant
concepts.summary: One number for a square matrix that says whether it is invertible, and by how much it scales area or volume. Three properties define it, and every other rule follows from them.

equations.says: The identity scales nothing.

equations.tex: \text{exchanging two rows flips the sign of } \det A
equations.says: Order matters, up to sign.

equations.tex: \det AB = \det A \,\det B, \qquad \det A^{\mathsf T} = \det A
equations.says: Determinants multiply, and ignore transposing.
A zero determinant means a flattened space.

metaphors.name: A photocopier's area dial
metaphors.says: A determinant of 2 doubles every area; 0 squashes the page flat, and nothing can unsquash it.

metaphors.name: A mirror
metaphors.says: A negative determinant flips orientation, the way a mirror turns a left hand into a right one.

metaphors.name: A volume knob for space
metaphors.says: One number says how much a transformation grows or shrinks everything it touches.

applications.name: Is it invertible?
applications.says: A zero determinant flags a system with no unique solution.

applications.name: Mirrored models
applications.says: Game engines check the sign of a transform's determinant to flip triangle winding when a model is mirrored.

applications.name: Change of variables
applications.says: The Jacobian determinant rescales areas in integrals and probability densities, as normalizing flows do in machine learning.

applications.name: Orientation tests
applications.says: The sign of a small determinant says whether a point is left or right of a line, the basic test of convex hulls and triangulations.

concepts.name: Determinant formulas and cofactors
concepts.summary: The determinant as a sum over one choice of entry from each row and column. Along any row it splits into entries times cofactors: smaller determinants with signs.

equations.tex: \det \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = ad - bc
equations.says: The two by two case.
Cofactor expansion along the first row.
A cofactor: the determinant with row i and column j removed, with a sign.

metaphors.name: Rooks on a board
metaphors.says: Each term of the big formula places one rook in every row and every column, none attacking another.

metaphors.name: Breaking a big decision into cases
metaphors.says: Pick the first row's entry, and what is left is a smaller version of the same problem.

metaphors.name: Nesting dolls
metaphors.says: Every cofactor holds a smaller determinant, which holds smaller ones still.

applications.name: Small inverses in games
applications.says: Engines invert 3×3 and 4×4 matrices with cofactors, which suits fixed sizes and fast hardware.

applications.name: The cross product
applications.says: The cross product is a cofactor expansion along a row of unit vectors.

applications.name: Closed forms
applications.says: Computer algebra systems use cofactors to give exact formulas in symbols.

applications.name: A lesson in growth
applications.says: The big formula has n! terms, so for large matrices elimination wins by a wide margin.

concepts.name: Cramer's rule, inverses and volume
concepts.summary: Determinants solve equations and invert matrices in closed form, and measure volume: the box a matrix's rows span has the determinant's size as its volume.

equations.says: Cramer's rule: B_j is A with column j replaced by b.
The inverse from the cofactors.
In the plane, the determinant is the area the unit square becomes.

metaphors.name: A pushed deck of cards
metaphors.says: Slide a deck sideways into a slant and its volume doesn't change: a shear keeps the determinant.

metaphors.name: A slanted garden plot
metaphors.says: The area of a parallelogram is the determinant of its two edges.

metaphors.name: Swapping a column
metaphors.says: To find one unknown, put the answer in place of its column and compare volumes.

applications.name: Ray–triangle hits
applications.says: Ray tracers find where a ray meets a triangle by solving a 3×3 system with Cramer's rule.

applications.name: Inside the triangle?
applications.says: Rasterizers decide whether a pixel is inside a triangle from the signs of three small determinants.

applications.name: Mesh volume
applications.says: Slicers for 3D printing sum signed volumes of tetrahedra to find how much material a model needs.

applications.name: Barycentric coordinates
applications.says: Blending colors and textures across a triangle uses ratios of areas, which are determinants.

concepts.name: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
concepts.summary: A direction a matrix only stretches, and how much it stretches it. Most vectors turn when multiplied by A; an eigenvector stays on its own line.

equations.says: A moves v along its own line, scaled by λ.
The λ that make this true are the eigenvalues.
The eigenvalues add up to the diagonal's sum and multiply to the determinant.

metaphors.name: A spinning globe
metaphors.says: Everything turns except the axis, which stays on its own line: an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1.

metaphors.name: Stretching dough
metaphors.says: Roll dough one way and some directions only get longer, without turning.

metaphors.name: A bridge's natural sway
metaphors.says: A structure has its own ways of vibrating, each at its own rate; push it at one and it responds strongly.

applications.name: PageRank
applications.says: Google's first ranking of the web was the leading eigenvector of a matrix of links.

applications.name: Vibration analysis
applications.says: Engineers find the eigenvalues of a building or an engine to keep its natural frequencies away from the ones it will meet.

applications.name: PCA
applications.says: The eigenvectors of a covariance matrix are the directions in which data varies most.

applications.name: Stability
applications.says: A linear system settles when every eigenvalue shrinks it, and blows up when one grows it.

concepts.name: Diagonalization and powers
concepts.summary: With a full set of eigenvectors, a matrix is just stretching along them. Powers are then easy: each eigenvalue is raised to the power. The Fibonacci numbers grow by the golden ratio this way.

equations.says: X holds the eigenvectors, Λ the eigenvalues on its diagonal.
Multiplying by A k times raises each eigenvalue to the k.
Fibonacci: the larger eigenvalue of [[1, 1], [1, 0]] takes over.

metaphors.name: The right coordinates
metaphors.says: A problem tangled in one set of axes is a list of separate, simple ones in the eigenvector axes.

metaphors.name: Separate savings accounts
metaphors.says: Each account grows by its own interest rate, and none affects the others.

metaphors.name: Untangling a knot of strings
metaphors.says: Once each string is on its own, pulling one doesn't move the rest.

applications.name: Recurrences
applications.says: Fibonacci-like sequences get closed forms, and their growth rates, from eigenvalues.

applications.name: Population models
applications.says: The long-run age mix of a population is read from the leading eigenvector of its growth matrix.

applications.name: Decoupled simulation
applications.says: Splitting a vibrating structure into its modes turns one big system into many small ones.

applications.name: Fast powers
applications.says: A high power of a matrix is just each eigenvalue raised to that power.

concepts.name: Differential equations and the matrix exponential
concepts.summary: A system of linear differential equations moves along the eigenvectors, each part growing or decaying at the rate its eigenvalue sets. The solution is the matrix exponential.

equations.says: The system: the rate of change depends linearly on where you are.
Each eigen-direction grows like e to its eigenvalue times t.
Stable: every part decays.

metaphors.name: Continuous compound interest
metaphors.says: Each eigen-direction grows like money compounded every instant, at its own rate.

metaphors.name: Heat between rooms
metaphors.says: Warm and cold rooms trade heat; the pattern of temperatures settles along the eigenvectors.

metaphors.name: A swing slowing down
metaphors.says: Friction makes each mode of motion fade at its own rate.

applications.name: Control systems
applications.says: Autopilots and cruise control model a vehicle as x' = Ax and predict it with the matrix exponential.

applications.name: Rotations
applications.says: The exponential of a skew-symmetric matrix is a rotation, the basis of how robotics and animation interpolate orientations.

applications.name: Reliability and queues
applications.says: Continuous-time Markov models of servers and machines evolve by an exponential of their rate matrix.

applications.name: Exact physics steps
applications.says: Simulations of linear springs and dampers can step exactly instead of approximating.

concepts.name: Markov matrices
concepts.summary: Columns of nonnegative numbers that each add to 1: the chances of moving from one state to another. Repeated steps settle into a steady state, the eigenvector for eigenvalue 1.

equations.says: One step of the chain.
The steady state: eigenvalue 1.
No eigenvalue is larger, so the other parts fade.

metaphors.name: A board game with dice
metaphors.says: Snakes and Ladders is a Markov chain: where you go next depends only on where you are.

metaphors.name: Tomorrow's weather
metaphors.says: If tomorrow depends only on today, the long-run share of sunny days is the steady state.

metaphors.name: Shuffling a deck
metaphors.says: Each riffle shuffle is a step; after enough of them every order is about equally likely.

applications.name: PageRank
applications.says: A random surfer clicking links spends time on each page in proportion to its rank.

applications.name: Text prediction
applications.says: Early autocomplete and text generators chose each next word from the one before it.

applications.name: Sampling
applications.says: Markov chain Monte Carlo explores probability distributions too complex to sample directly.

applications.name: Speech and biology
applications.says: Hidden Markov models recognize speech and find genes in DNA.

concepts.name: Fourier series
concepts.summary: A function written as a sum of sines and cosines, which are orthogonal to each other just as the axes are. Each coefficient is a projection onto one of them.

equations.tex: f(x) = a_0 + a_1\cos x + b_1\sin x + a_2\cos 2x + b_2\sin 2x + \cdots
equations.says: A function as a combination of waves.
The coefficient is the projection of f onto sin kx.

metaphors.name: Hearing a chord
metaphors.says: Your ear splits a sound into its notes and how loud each is.

metaphors.name: A graphic equalizer
metaphors.says: Each slider is one coefficient, how much of one frequency is in the sound.

metaphors.name: Ocean swells
metaphors.says: A choppy sea is many smooth waves of different lengths added together.

applications.name: Audio compression
applications.says: MP3 and AAC store a sound by its frequencies and spend fewest bits on the ones the ear notices least.

applications.name: Image compression
applications.says: JPEG writes each block of an image in a basis of cosines.

applications.name: Heat and waves
applications.says: Fourier invented the series to solve how heat spreads; physics simulations still do.

applications.name: Synthesizers
applications.says: Additive synthesis builds a sound from sines, one coefficient at a time.

concepts.name: Symmetric matrices
concepts.summary: A matrix equal to its transpose. Its eigenvalues are real and its eigenvectors can be chosen at right angles, so it is a sum of stretches along perpendicular directions.

equations.says: Symmetric.
The spectral theorem: orthonormal eigenvectors in Q, real eigenvalues in Λ.

metaphors.name: A mileage chart
metaphors.says: Boston to New York is as far as New York to Boston.

metaphors.name: Mutual friendship
metaphors.says: Friends on a network are friends both ways; followers are not, and that matrix is not symmetric.

metaphors.name: A squeezed ball
metaphors.says: Press a rubber ball and it stretches along perpendicular directions, with no twist.

applications.name: Covariance
applications.says: How features vary together is a symmetric matrix, and PCA reads it through its perpendicular eigenvectors.

applications.name: Undirected networks
applications.says: Graph Laplacians are symmetric, which makes spectral clustering and graph drawing work.

applications.name: Optimization
applications.says: The Hessian of second derivatives is symmetric and describes the shape of a function near a point.

applications.name: Physics simulation
applications.says: Springs pull equally both ways, so stiffness matrices are symmetric, and faster solvers apply.

concepts.name: Complex matrices and the fast Fourier transform
concepts.summary: With complex numbers, transposing comes with conjugating. The Fourier matrix is built from powers of a complex root of 1, and the FFT multiplies by it in n log n steps instead of n².

equations.says: The conjugate transpose, which takes the transpose's place.
The Fourier matrix: powers of the n-th root of 1.
The FFT splits F_n into two copies of F_{n/2}, again and again.

metaphors.name: Hands on a clock
metaphors.says: The powers of a root of 1 are evenly spaced points around a circle, like the hours.

metaphors.name: Divide and conquer
metaphors.says: Like sorting a deck by splitting it in halves, the FFT splits a signal into evens and odds and reuses the work.

metaphors.name: A prism
metaphors.says: White light goes in, and its colors fan out: a signal goes in, and its frequencies come out.

applications.name: Wireless
applications.says: Wi-Fi, 4G and 5G send data on many frequencies at once and separate them with an FFT.

applications.name: Multiplying huge numbers
applications.says: Fast multiplication of polynomials and big integers, as in computer algebra, runs through the FFT.

applications.name: Fast blurs and filters
applications.says: Image and audio filters convolve by multiplying spectra, which is quick for big kernels.

applications.name: Medical imaging
applications.says: MRI scanners measure frequencies, and an inverse FFT turns them into a picture.

concepts.name: Positive definite matrices
concepts.summary: A symmetric matrix whose energy is positive for every nonzero vector. Its graph is a bowl, so it has a minimum, and every test agrees: positive eigenvalues, pivots and leading determinants.

equations.says: Positive energy.
Equivalently, every eigenvalue is positive.
Every positive definite matrix is one, with A's columns independent.

metaphors.name: A bowl
metaphors.says: A marble dropped anywhere rolls to the one lowest point.

metaphors.name: A spring
metaphors.says: Pull it any way and it stores energy and pushes back.

metaphors.name: A valley, not a mountain pass
metaphors.says: At a pass the ground rises one way and falls another; that is indefinite.

applications.name: Optimization
applications.says: A positive definite Hessian means a true minimum; Newton's method and convex optimization rely on it.

applications.name: Kernel methods
applications.says: Support vector machines and Gaussian processes need positive (semi)definite kernel matrices.

applications.name: Cholesky factorization
applications.says: Solves positive definite systems about twice as fast as LU, and is used throughout simulation.

applications.name: Correlated randomness
applications.says: Simulations draw correlated random numbers by multiplying independent ones by a Cholesky factor.

concepts.name: Similar matrices and Jordan form
concepts.summary: Two matrices are similar when one is the other seen in a different basis. They share eigenvalues; the Jordan form is the simplest matrix in each family.

equations.says: Similar: A, seen through the change of basis M.
The same eigenvalues, with the eigenvectors changed by M.

metaphors.name: One song, two keys
metaphors.says: Transposed to another key, every interval stays the same.

metaphors.name: Two languages
metaphors.says: The same sentence in French and English: different words, the same meaning.

metaphors.name: Lowest terms
metaphors.says: The Jordan form is to similar matrices what 1/2 is to 2/4, 3/6 and 50/100.

applications.name: Rotating about an object's center
applications.says: Graphics moves the object to the origin, rotates, and moves it back: B⁻¹AB.

applications.name: Control design
applications.says: Engineers change a system's coordinates to a standard form where the controller is easy to design.

applications.name: Same system, new labels
applications.says: Matrices with different eigenvalues can't be the same system relabeled, a quick first check.

applications.name: Resonance
applications.says: A Jordan block explains why some systems grow like t·e^{λt} instead of a plain exponential.

concepts.name: The singular value decomposition
concepts.summary: Every matrix, square or not, turns a set of perpendicular directions into another set of perpendicular directions, stretched. It rotates, stretches along the axes, and rotates again.

equations.says: Orthonormal V and U, with the singular values on Σ's diagonal.
Each right singular vector lands on a left one, stretched by σ_i.
A sum of rank one pieces, largest first.

metaphors.name: Pressing clay
metaphors.says: Any press of a ball of clay is a turn, a squash along the axes, and another turn.

metaphors.name: Layers by importance
metaphors.says: A table broken into simple layers, the strongest first, like summarizing a book by its biggest themes.

metaphors.name: A dance step
metaphors.says: Rotate, stretch, rotate: every matrix does the same three moves.

applications.name: Image compression
applications.says: Keeping the largest singular values keeps the picture, with a fraction of the numbers.

applications.name: Recommenders
applications.says: Matrix factorization of ratings was central to the Netflix Prize.

applications.name: Search by meaning
applications.says: Latent semantic analysis finds documents about the same topic even when they share no words.

applications.name: Aligning shapes
applications.says: The Kabsch algorithm aligns two point clouds, as in 3D scanning and comparing protein structures, with one SVD.

concepts.name: Linear transformations
concepts.summary: A map that respects combinations: the image of a combination is the same combination of the images. Every one is a matrix, whose columns are where the basis vectors go.

equations.says: Linear: it keeps lines straight and the origin fixed.
The matrix's columns are the images of the basis.

metaphors.name: Graph paper on a rubber sheet
metaphors.says: Stretch the sheet so grid lines stay straight, evenly spaced, and through the same center.

metaphors.name: Where your hands go
metaphors.says: Know where east and north land and you know where everything lands.

metaphors.name: A tidy funhouse mirror
metaphors.says: It may stretch or tilt, but never bends a straight line.

applications.name: Every graphics transform
applications.says: Rotation, scaling and shear are matrices, and with homogeneous coordinates so is moving.

applications.name: Photo editing
applications.says: Skew, scale and perspective tools warp an image by a transformation.

applications.name: Automatic differentiation
applications.says: A derivative is the best linear map near a point, and autodiff composes them.

applications.name: Neural network layers
applications.says: Each layer is a linear transformation followed by a bend.

concepts.name: Change of basis and compression
concepts.summary: The same vector has different coordinates in different bases. Image compression changes to a basis, like waves or wavelets, where most coordinates are small, and keeps only the large ones.

equations.says: c holds the coordinates of x in the basis of W's columns.
The same transformation, written in the new basis.

metaphors.name: Currencies
metaphors.says: One price in dollars and in euros: the value is the same and only the numbers change.

metaphors.name: Address or coordinates
metaphors.says: A street address and a latitude and longitude name the same house.

metaphors.name: Sheet music
metaphors.says: Writing a tune as notes needs far fewer numbers than writing down the air pressure at every instant.

applications.name: Compression
applications.says: JPEG uses cosines, JPEG 2000 wavelets and MP3 frequencies, keeping only the big coordinates.

applications.name: Video color
applications.says: Video moves RGB into brightness and color (YCbCr) and keeps more detail in brightness, which the eye sees best.

applications.name: Frames in graphics
applications.says: Every object, the world and the camera each have a basis, and rendering moves between them.

applications.name: PCA
applications.says: Rewriting data in the basis of its principal directions puts most of the variation in a few coordinates.

concepts.name: Left, right and pseudoinverses
concepts.summary: A matrix that isn't square still has inverses from one side when its rank is full. The pseudoinverse inverts what can be inverted: it maps the column space back to the row space.

equations.says: A left inverse, when the columns are independent.
The pseudoinverse: invert each nonzero singular value.

metaphors.name: Undoing a shadow
metaphors.says: A shadow can't tell you an object's height, so pick the simplest object that would cast it.

metaphors.name: Least effort
metaphors.says: Among all the ways to reach a spot, take the one that moves the least.

metaphors.name: A careful translator
metaphors.says: Some words have no equivalent, so give the closest meaning and leave out what can't be said.

applications.name: Regression
applications.says: The pseudoinverse gives the least-squares fit, even when the data has redundant features.

applications.name: Inverse kinematics
applications.says: Robots and animated characters find the smallest joint motions that move a hand where it should go.

applications.name: Drones and spacecraft
applications.says: Control allocation splits a desired force among many thrusters or rotors.

applications.name: Underdetermined problems
applications.says: With fewer equations than unknowns, it picks the solution of least length.
